title: Better Than the Chimp
book: Superforecasting: The Art and Science of Prediction
author: Philip Tetlock and Dan Gardner
wiifm: Every week you make bets about the future: this client will renew, this hire will work, this month will hit target. Almost nobody checks how good those judgements are. This is the story of a psychologist who got annoyed that the experts on television were never marked, spent twenty years marking them, then ran the largest forecasting contest ever held and watched retired amateurs beat the professionals. After three days on what cannot be known, it is the hopeful corrective. You will come away with a simple, scored method for making your own guesses measurably better.

ch.h: A boy who wanted to know who was right
b: Philip Tetlock was born in Toronto in 1954 and grew up in Winnipeg, a long way from the centres of power he would later study. He was drawn early to psychology, and in particular to a question that sounds simple and is not: how do people decide what to believe, and how would you ever know if they were right?

He studied at the University of British Columbia, then went to Yale for his doctorate, which he completed in 1979. His early work was on how people reason about politics, how they justify their views to others, and how being held to account changes the way they think. That last idea, accountability, would turn out to be the hinge of his whole career.

He took a post at the University of California at Berkeley. It was the early nineteen-eighties, the height of the late Cold War, and the airwaves were full of confident people explaining what the Soviet Union would do next.

He was not a contrarian by nature. Colleagues describe him as courteous, careful and almost painfully fair to the people whose views he tested. What drove him was a scientist's discomfort with claims that could never be checked. If a doctor's diagnoses were never compared with what the patient turned out to have, nobody would trust the doctor. Yet in politics and economics, the most influential predictions in the world went unmarked year after year.
Keep that picture in mind: a young psychologist interested in accountability, surrounded by experts who were never held to account for anything. It is the itch that produced this book.
ch.cap: Young Tetlock wonders who checks the TV pundit's forecast

b: In 1984 Tetlock sat on a committee of the National Research Council looking at how American and Soviet behaviour might lead to nuclear war. Around the table were some of the most distinguished experts in the field. What struck him was not that their predictions differed. It was that nobody ever went back to check who had been right.

Forecasts were made in language slippery enough that no outcome could contradict them: a distinct possibility, could well, may before long. When events arrived, the forecaster explained either why he had been right or why he had been nearly right, and moved on. A year later Mikhail Gorbachev came to power, and within a few years experts who had been confident the Soviet system was stable were explaining why its collapse had been inevitable.
That is Taleb's narrative fallacy, watched in real time by someone who decided to do something about it.

Tetlock's plan was patient and unglamorous. He would ask experts to make specific predictions, with numbers attached, about questions that would definitely resolve. Then he would wait, and score them.
ch.cap: Experts hedge on nuclear war while Tetlock takes notes

b: Over the next two decades, ending in 2003, Tetlock recruited 284 people who made their living commenting on or advising about political and economic trends: academics, government officials, journalists. He gathered something like twenty-eight thousand predictions from them, each one specific and scorable.

He published the results in 2005 as Expert Political Judgment, and they were bruising. Beyond the short term, the average expert did little better than chance. Tetlock summed it up with a line that has followed him ever since: the average expert was roughly as accurate as a dart-throwing chimpanzee.

He has spent years explaining what that line does not mean. There was no chimpanzee; it was a vivid way of saying random. And the finding was not that expertise is worthless. Experts did beat undergraduates and simple trend lines in the short run. The real findings were that expertise stopped helping surprisingly quickly, and that fame, credentials and access to secret information bore no relationship at all to accuracy.
Something did predict accuracy, though. It was not what the experts knew. It was how they thought.

The book landed quietly in academic circles and loudly everywhere else. Journalists loved the chimpanzee, and many reported it as proof that experts are useless, which was the opposite of Tetlock's careful conclusion. He found himself, a little ruefully, a victim of exactly the oversimplification he had been studying. But the study had shown something precious: that judgement could be measured, and that once it was measured, real differences between people appeared.
ch.cap: A dart-throwing chimp ties with the average expert

b: Tetlock borrowed his categories from the philosopher Isaiah Berlin's 1953 essay The Hedgehog and the Fox, which took them from a fragment of the ancient Greek poet Archilochus: the fox knows many things, but the hedgehog knows one big thing.

The hedgehogs in his study organised everything around one commanding idea, a theory of markets or power or history, and pushed every situation through it. They were fluent, confident and memorable. On longer-range questions they did worse than chance, and as they became more famous their confidence rose.

The foxes drew ideas from many places, held them loosely, tolerated contradiction and spoke in qualifications. Their forecasts were undramatic and moved in small steps as news arrived. They did measurably better.

And here is the twist that links to Tuesday. Hedgehogs are rewarded. A producer booking a guest wants a clear story and a bold claim, not someone who says it depends on three things and puts it at about a third. Tetlock found that media prominence went with worse accuracy. The incentives of public commentary select against the very trait that produces good answers, which is one of Donella Meadows' system traps dressed up as a career.
ch.cap: The hedgehog gets the spotlight; the fox scans many paths

b: By the late two-thousands the American intelligence community had suffered a humiliation over Iraq's supposed weapons of mass destruction. Its research agency, IARPA, did something unusual. In 2011 it launched a four-year forecasting tournament. Several university teams were given the same stream of questions, all of which had to resolve clearly within months. Will this leader still be in office on this date? Will this currency fall below that level? Will these talks produce a signed agreement?

Tetlock, now at the University of Pennsylvania, ran a team with his wife and fellow psychologist Barbara Mellers. They called it the Good Judgment Project, and they did something no rival thought worth doing: they recruited thousands of ordinary volunteers from the public.

Every forecast was scored with the Brier score, invented by the meteorologist Glenn Brier in 1950. It measures the squared gap between the probability you gave and what actually happened. Zero is perfect. On the version the project used, two is being completely and confidently wrong. The beauty of it is that it punishes being wrong and being overconfident at once, and it makes vagueness impossible, because you cannot score a forecast that has no number in it.

The Good Judgment Project won, and won by such a margin that IARPA eventually dropped the other teams. In the first year it beat the agency's own control group by around sixty per cent, and in the second year by more. The volunteers were not paid much, received no secret briefings and worked from home in their spare time. What they were given was feedback: after every question closed, they could see exactly how good their numbers had been.
ch.cap: Volunteers forecast from home, every answer Brier-scored

b: Inside the winning team, Tetlock found something even more striking. A small group of forecasters, roughly the top two per cent, were dramatically better than everyone else. And they stayed better the following year, when luck alone should have pulled them back towards the middle. He called them superforecasters.

One was Bill Flack, a retired irrigation specialist who had worked for the United States Department of Agriculture in Nebraska. Another was Doug Lorch, a retired IBM programmer. They had no security clearance, no sources inside foreign ministries, no research budget. What they had was an internet connection, a habit of breaking problems apart, and a willingness to put a number on their beliefs and be scored on every one.

The figure that later spread was that the project's forecasts beat those of intelligence analysts with access to classified information by about thirty per cent. That comparison was reported by a journalist and never published in a form outsiders could check, so treat it with care. But nobody has offered a good reason to doubt its direction.

Nor were the superforecasters geniuses. They were bright, scoring well above average on intelligence tests, but not exceptional. What marked them out more strongly was a habit of reflection: a willingness to stop, override the first tempting answer, and actually work the problem.
ch.cap: A retired Nebraska irrigation man forecasts at his kitchen table

b: The methods are the treasure of the book, and they are reassuringly mechanical. Take a question the tournament really asked: would tests on the exhumed remains of the Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat find signs of polonium poisoning?

An ordinary forecaster consults a general feeling about Middle Eastern politics and conspiracy theories and says probably not. A superforecaster refuses to answer the question as asked and breaks it into parts. Is polonium even detectable after this many years, given how quickly it decays? If it is, how many different ways could it have got there: poisoning by any of the many people with a motive, or contamination of the remains after his death by someone hoping to cast blame? And with more than one country's scientists testing, does a positive from either of them count? Each part can be researched and bounded.

This is Enrico Fermi's old trick, which he used to estimate how many piano tuners there were in Chicago by multiplying guessable pieces. The errors in the pieces partly cancel, while a single gut guess has nothing to cancel against.

Then come the other habits. Triage, spending effort only on questions where work changes the answer. Start with the outside view, the base rate for cases like this one, before the inside view of this case's details. Update often, in small steps, rather than refusing to move or lurching on a headline. Keep precision: the project found that rounding forecasts to the nearest ten per cent measurably hurt accuracy. Argue in teams, then nudge the combined average a little towards the nearer extreme, because each individual has hedged for doubts the group no longer has.
ch.cap: The polonium question broken into small, checkable branches

b: In 2015, with the journalist Dan Gardner, Tetlock turned all this into Superforecasting. Its appendix offers ten commandments, followed by an eleventh telling you not to treat the ten as commandments. The spirit beneath them is what he calls perpetual beta, a phrase from software for a product that is never finished. Treat every belief as your current best estimate with a revision date, not a possession to defend.

Superforecasters, he found, scored high on what psychologists call actively open-minded thinking. They saw their beliefs as hypotheses to be tested rather than treasures to be guarded. Changing their minds was not a defeat. It was the job.

You can start this week. Keep a one-page forecast log. Each time you make a judgement that will resolve, this client renews, this quote converts, this hire works out, we hit this revenue by this date, write the claim, the date it resolves and a probability. Not I think so. Seventy per cent. Then record what happened.

Two months of this will tell you more about your judgement than years of reflection. Many owners discover something specific and expensive: that their sixty per cents come in at forty, or that they are well calibrated about operations and wildly optimistic about anything involving another person's enthusiasm. And before any new launch, ask the outside-view question owner-operators skip: of the last five new things we tried, how many are still running and profitable? That ratio belongs in the decision before any excitement does.
ch.cap: An owner writes seventy per cent in his forecast log

ch.h: What the tournament could not ask
b: Read the book with three honest reservations.

First, tournament questions had to resolve within months and be precisely worded. That rules out exactly the events Taleb cares about. Nobody could ask the tournament to forecast a pandemic starting in an unknown city in an unknown year, because it could not be scored. Taleb says the class of scorable questions leaves out the events that shape history, and he is right. Tetlock says most decisions we actually make are in the scorable class, and he is right too.

Second, the superforecaster label suggests a separate breed of person. The writer Scott Alexander, among others, pointed out that performance looks more like a continuous spread with a long tail. The persistence of the top performers from year to year is real evidence against pure luck, but the name is marketing as well as science.

Third, skill may not travel as well as the book's tone implies. In 2023 a large study called the Forecasting Collaborative, led by Igor Grossmann, asked social scientists to forecast social change through the pandemic years and found that most did no better than simple statistical models or lay crowds. Forecasting skill, it seems, depends heavily on the domain.
ch.cap: Near signposts are clear; beyond the fog, an unscorable swan

b: So where does this leave the week? After Taleb, Meadows and Perrow, Tetlock is the reminder that a great deal of the world is more knowable than gloomy rhetoric suggests, provided you do the unglamorous work of writing numbers down and checking them.

The way to hold the two views together is to sort your questions before choosing your method. Where feedback arrives within months and the question is clear, forecast, and score yourself ruthlessly. Will this client renew? Will this campaign pay back by March? Those are tournament questions, and you can get better at them. Where the question is long-range, vague or sits in Extremistan, stop forecasting and go back to Monday's advice: cap the downside so you no longer need the forecast.

Tetlock's life story is, in the end, a story about accountability. A young psychologist noticed that confident people were never marked, and spent four decades building the marking scheme. The result was not a magic method. It was the discovery that ordinary, careful people who keep score improve, and that famous, confident people who do not keep score mostly do not.

A retired irrigation specialist in Nebraska, with a spreadsheet and the humility to write down seventy per cent and be checked, beat people with security clearances. You can do the same with your own business, starting with one page and one number.
ch.cap: Sorting questions: forecast the clear, cap the wild

take: Unscored forecasts never improve. Start a one-page log with the claim, a probability, a resolution date and the outcome.
Fame, credentials and access did not predict accuracy, and media prominence went with worse results. Ask any adviser for their track record.
Gather views from several sources, hold them loosely, and accept that careful answers sound less impressive than bold ones.
Put a precise number on it
Probably cannot be scored, but sixty-five per cent can. Rounding to the nearest ten measurably reduced accuracy.
Split a hard question into smaller ones you can research, as with the Arafat polonium question. Errors in the parts partly cancel.
Before looking at your case's details, ask how often cases like it succeed, including your own last five launches.
Refusing to move and lurching on one headline are the same mistake. Nudge your estimate as evidence arrives.
Forecast where feedback comes quickly and questions are clear. Where it does not, cap your downside instead.
recall: What did Tetlock's study of 284 experts actually find?

Beyond the short term the average expert was close to chance, and fame, credentials and access did not predict accuracy. Experts did beat students and simple trend lines in the short run, and thinking style, fox rather than hedgehog, was what predicted accuracy.
Why is the Brier score so important to the method?

It measures the squared gap between stated probability and outcome, punishing both error and overconfidence. It also makes vague forecasts impossible, because a forecast without a number cannot be scored.
What were the Good Judgment Project and the superforecasters?

It was Tetlock and Barbara Mellers' team in IARPA's tournament from 2011, using public volunteers, and it won decisively. The superforecasters were roughly the top two per cent, who stayed at the top year after year.
How does breaking a question into parts help?

It turns one unanswerable judgement into several smaller ones you can research and bound. Errors in the parts are partly independent and partly cancel, while a single gut guess has nothing to cancel against.
What are the main limits of the book's findings?

Tournament questions must resolve quickly and clearly, so they exclude long-range black swans. The superforecaster label may overstate a continuous spread, and the 2023 Forecasting Collaborative suggests forecasting skill varies strongly by domain.
note: Expert Political Judgment (2005) reports the 284 experts and roughly 28,000 forecasts. The thirty per cent advantage over intelligence analysts was reported by David Ignatius in The Washington Post and has not been published for outside scrutiny. Tetlock's Brier scoring used the original version ranging from zero to two. Critiques include Scott Alexander's review and the Forecasting Collaborative, Grossmann and colleagues, Nature Human Behaviour, 2023.
words: The match between the confidence you state and how often you turn out to be right.
A well-calibrated forecaster's seventy per cent calls come true about seven times in ten, which is exactly what the Brier score in Tetlock's tournament rewarded.

Tetlock noticed that expert forecasts were full of equivocation, phrases like a distinct possibility that no outcome could ever contradict.
The act of predicting the future, often with a hint of self-importance.
Tetlock's twenty-year study put professional prognostication to the test and found the average expert, beyond the short term, little better than chance.
The level of fine detail or precision in a measurement or judgement.
The project found granularity mattered: rounding forecasts to the nearest ten per cent measurably reduced their accuracy.
In statistics, the tendency of unusually high or low results to drift back towards the average next time.
Superforecasters impressed Tetlock because they resisted regression to the mean, staying near the top the following year when luck alone should have pulled them back.

The irrigation man beats the spies

After the Iraq weapons failure, the American intelligence research agency IARPA launched a forecasting tournament in 2011. Rival university teams got the same questions. Tetlock and his wife Barbara Mellers did something nobody else bothered with: they recruited thousands of ordinary volunteers. Their Good Judgment Project won so decisively that IARPA dropped the other teams. Among its stars was Bill Flack, a retired irrigation specialist from Nebraska, with no clearance and no secret sources, just an internet connection and the habit of writing down a number and being scored. Can polonium still be detected after this many years, given how fast it decays? If so, how many ways could it get there, poisoning or deliberate contamination after death? It is Enrico Fermi's trick for guessing Chicago's piano tuners: errors in the pieces partly cancel, while one gut guess has nothing to cancel against.
biz: A forecast log for every case

This week, when a secured-loan enquiry reaches application, have whoever handles it write one number in the CRM: the chance it completes, say sixty-five per cent, with the expected date. Record what happens. After two months, compare by channel and by person: do Google cases called at seventy complete seven times in ten, or four? Keep the scores internal and use them to plan cash, staffing and spend. Never turn them into anything a customer hears as a likely approval, since lenders decide and Consumer Duty requires clear, fair communication. The aim is honest judgement, not a sales tool.
Score the people who forecast for you

Platforms, agencies, lead suppliers and software vendors all make predictions: this change will cut cost per lead by a third, this audience will convert. Tetlock found reputation told you nothing about accuracy. Start a simple sheet: who said it, the specific claim, the date it resolves, and the result. Ask suppliers to put a number on any promise before you agree to spend. Review the sheet each quarter and give more weight to the sources with good records. Before any new launch, also take the outside view: of the last five new campaigns or pages, how many are still running and paying back?
connects: Kahneman's split between fast intuition and slow reasoning explains why superforecasters, who stop and override their first answer, beat people who trust their gut, and his outside view is the base rate habit Tetlock teaches.
Dalio's believability-weighted decision making and Tetlock's scored forecasts share one idea: give weight to people according to their checked track record, not their confidence.
Taleb argues that the scorable questions in a tournament leave out the rare shocks that shape history, which is the main limit on Tetlock's optimism.
recap:
Philip Tetlock was born in Toronto in nineteen fifty-four and grew up in Winnipeg. He became a psychologist fascinated by one idea: accountability, and how being held to account changes the way we think. In the early nineteen-eighties, sitting on a committee about the risk of nuclear war, he noticed something odd. The distinguished experts around the table made predictions all the time, in language slippery enough to survive any outcome, and nobody ever went back to check who had been right.

So he checked. Over about twenty years he gathered some twenty-eight thousand specific, scorable predictions from two hundred and eighty-four professional experts. In two thousand and five he reported that, beyond the short term, the average expert did little better than chance, roughly as well as a dart-throwing chimpanzee. Journalists loved the line and misread it. Tetlock's real finding was subtler. Fame and credentials did not predict accuracy, but a style of thinking did. Hedgehogs, who know one big thing, were confident, memorable and often wrong. Foxes, who know many things and hold them loosely, did better, and were invited onto television less.

Then came the real test. After the intelligence failure over Iraq, the American research agency known as IARPA launched a forecasting tournament in two thousand and eleven. Tetlock and his wife Barbara Mellers ran the Good Judgment Project, recruiting thousands of ordinary volunteers and scoring every forecast with the Brier score, which punishes both error and overconfidence. They won so convincingly that the other teams were dropped. Within the team, roughly the top two per cent, people like a retired irrigation specialist from Nebraska, stayed better year after year. Tetlock called them superforecasters.

Their methods are learnable. Break a hard question into smaller parts you can research. Start with the base rate for cases like this one, then adjust for the details. Update often, in small steps. Be precise, because rounding to the nearest ten per cent hurt accuracy. And treat every belief as a draft, in what he called perpetual beta.

There are limits. Tournament questions had to resolve within months, which leaves out the rare shocks that Taleb cares about, and later research suggests forecasting skill depends heavily on the field. So sort your questions first. Forecast and keep score where feedback is quick, and cap your downside where it is not.

The line to remember: judgement that is never scored never improves, so write down the number and check it.
